text:
Two months is closer. I gave you the popular figure without telling you the research doesn't back it.

The 21 days traces to Maxwell Maltz, a plastic surgeon, who wrote in his 1960 book Psycho-Cybernetics that "it requires a minimum of about 21 days for an old mental image to dissolve and a new one to jell," after watching patients adjust to physical changes. That was a minimum based on his patients, and it got repeated as the time a habit takes.

The study usually cited for a real number is Lally and colleagues at UCL (2010). Ninety-six volunteers each picked a daily behavior to attach to a cue, like eating fruit with lunch or running 15 minutes before dinner, and rated how automatic it felt every day for 12 weeks. For those whose ratings followed a clear leveling-off curve, the median time to level off was 66 days, and individuals ranged from 18 days to a projected 254. One missed day made little difference, though many misses, even spread out, lowered how automatic it eventually got.

A 2024 review of 20 studies found four that reported timing: medians of 59 to 66 days, means of 106 to 154 days, and individuals from 4 to 335 days. Lally's behaviors were eating, drinking and exercise, and the review covers health habits, so for journaling these numbers are a rough guide. I'd plan on about two months of showing up, and with a spread that wide, a slower start is ordinary.

What's something you already do every morning without fail? That's a good place to attach the journaling.

Yes, we can do a short one, and you set the pace. You don't need to know why you feel small before we start. We'll begin by getting steady where you are, and only then turn toward the small feeling, from whatever distance feels okay. You can stop or slow down whenever you want.

Two quick questions first, so I can fit this to you. A few words each is plenty.

When you say "small" right now, what are you noticing: something in your body, a picture, words, a mood, an urge, or something hard to name? Vague is fine, and so is "no words."

And in ordinary daily thinking, how often are actual silent words or sentences present in your mind: rarely/never, sometimes, often, or almost constantly? And if you choose to, can you deliberately think a sentence silently? There's no right answer.

text:
Yes, we can keep it short. You don't have to know why you feel small to start; if the why turns out to matter, we can come back to it. You can pause or stop whenever you want.

Two quick things first, so I fit this to you instead of guessing. There are no right answers, and short replies are fine.

First, take a breath and glance around wherever you are. Then, when you say "small," what do you actually notice right now? It might be something in your body, a picture, an urge, actual words, a memory, or something hard to name. "Not sure" is a fine answer.

Second, in ordinary daily thinking, how often are actual silent words or sentences present in your mind—rarely/never, sometimes, often, or almost constantly? And if you choose to, can you deliberately think a sentence silently?

Once I have both, I'll suggest a first small step.
